query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding approximately 5 at% tungsten to a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy will promote the formation of fine, tungsten-enriched precipitates that hinder dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding at elevated temperatures, thereby enhancing high-temperature yield strength and creep resistance relative to the tungsten-free alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy where titanium and nickel are the primary constituents with at least three additional elements (each present at 5–35 at%) and without tungsten.
generation.intervention: Incorporate roughly 5 at% tungsten into the alloy composition during synthesis.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature mechanical testing (approximately 700–900°C) conducted under an inert atmosphere, with the material processed to ensure a uniform microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of fine, tungsten-enriched precipitates distributed within the alloy matrix.
generation.mechanism: The tungsten addition facilitates precipitation strengthening by forming stable precipitates that pin dislocations and restrict grain-boundary sliding during high-temperature deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The tungsten-added alloy is expected to exhibit a measurable enhancement in high-temperature yield strength and improved creep resistance compared to the baseline alloy without tungsten.
generation.baseline: The titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy synthesized without tungsten addition.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable when the alloy adheres to high-entropy criteria (each element between 5–35 at%), is processed to achieve a homogeneous microstructure, and is tested under elevated temperatures in the 700–900°C range.
generation.uncertainty: While precipitation strengthening is anticipated, the extent of the improvement may vary based on processing conditions and the exact precipitate characteristics, and precise quantitative benefits remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy specimens with identical base compositions: one set with an added ~5 at% tungsten and one set without tungsten. Ensure both groups undergo the same thermomechanical processing to achieve similar microstructures. Conduct high-temperature mechanical tests, such as tensile or creep testing, at approximately 800°C under an inert atmosphere.
measurements: Creep rate under a constant load at high temperature
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to confirm the presence and distribution of tungsten-enriched precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-containing alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in yield strength and/or a reduction in creep rate relative to the tungsten-free baseline, or if TEM analysis does not reveal the formation of the expected fine, tungsten-enriched precipitates, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a minor amount of tungsten (~2–5 at%) to a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy, followed by a controlled aging heat treatment, will form fine, coherent tungsten–titanium precipitates that improve elevated-temperature strength and creep resistance compared to the same alloy without this intervention.
drafts.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy where titanium and nickel are the primary constituents along with three or more additional elements in the 5–35 at% range, produced without tungsten addition or specialized aging treatment.
drafts.intervention: Add ~2–5 at% tungsten during alloy synthesis and apply a post-synthesis aging treatment at an optimized temperature (e.g., 600–700°C) for a set duration to promote precipitate formation.
drafts.conditions: Mechanical testing under elevated-temperature conditions (600–800°C) representative of extreme environmental applications.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of nanoscale, coherent tungsten–titanium precipitates distributed uniformly throughout the alloy matrix.
drafts.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening: The nano-precipitates hinder dislocation movement and grain-boundary sliding at high temperatures, thereby enhancing yield strength and creep resistance.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The treated, tungsten-doped alloy will exhibit a statistically significant improvement in elevated-temperature mechanical properties (e.g., >10% increase in yield strength and reduced creep rates) compared to the identical alloy without tungsten addition and aging.
drafts.baseline: The titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy synthesized without tungsten and without the post-synthesis aging treatment.
drafts.boundary: This intervention is applicable for high-entropy alloys within the compositional limits (five or more elements at 5–35 at% each) operating under temperatures between 600°C and 800°C, with tungsten additions maintained between 2–5 at%.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) the intervention group with ~2–5 at% tungsten added and subjected to the specified aging treatment, and (2) a control group synthesized without tungsten and without the post-synthesis aging. Subject both groups to identical mechanical tests at elevated temperatures (e.g., tensile or creep tests at 700°C). Use microscopy (TEM/SEM) to analyze the presence and distribution of nano-precipitates.
measurements: Creep strain or creep rate under constant load
Microstructural evidence of coherent tungsten–titanium precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-doped and aged alloy does not show at least a 10% improvement in yield strength or a reduction in creep rate compared to the control, or if microscopy fails to reveal the intended nano-scale precipitates, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a modest amount of tungsten (around 5 at%) to a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy will improve its elevated-temperature mechanical properties compared to the same alloy without tungsten.
drafts.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy meeting the compositional definition, where titanium and nickel are the primary constituents along with at least three other elements, and tungsten is absent.
drafts.intervention: Introduce 5 at% tungsten into the alloy composition while maintaining the overall high-entropy alloy criteria.
drafts.conditions: Elevated-temperature testing (approximately 700–900°C) under controlled atmospheres (e.g., inert gas) with similar thermomechanical processing histories to ensure consistent microstructures.
drafts.structural_mediator: Fine, tungsten-enriched precipitates that form preferentially at grain boundaries.
drafts.mechanism: Tungsten addition promotes the formation of fine, stable precipitates at grain boundaries, which impede grain boundary sliding and dislocation motion. This dispersion strengthening mechanism is expected to enhance both yield strength and creep resistance at high temperatures.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The tungsten-added alloy should exhibit a higher yield strength and lower creep rate at elevated temperatures compared to the baseline alloy without tungsten.
drafts.baseline: Titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy without tungsten addition.
drafts.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated to occur within the operating temperature range of roughly 700–900°C, and with tungsten additions kept near 5 at% to prevent formation of brittle intermetallic phases; the alloy must still adhere to the high-entropy criteria of at least five elements with comparable atomic radii.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one control set with the baseline titanium- and nickel-primary composition and one experimental set with an added 5 at% tungsten. Ensure both sets undergo identical thermomechanical processing to achieve similar microstructural homogeneity. Conduct isothermal tensile and creep tests at 800°C under an inert atmosphere.
measurements: Creep rate under a constant load
TEM analysis to verify the formation and distribution of tungsten-enriched precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the tungsten-added alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., less than a 10% increase in yield strength or less than a 15% reduction in creep rate) compared to the baseline, or if TEM analysis reveals that tungsten addition results in deleterious brittle phases.

drafts.hypothesis: A controlled thermal aging treatment that induces nano‐scale intermetallic (gamma) precipitates in a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy will improve its elevated-temperature mechanical properties compared to the alloy in the as-solution-annealed state.
drafts.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy formulated with titanium and nickel as the primary constituents along with three additional elements (each between 5–35 at%) to satisfy the high-entropy criterion, prepared by solution annealing and exhibiting a homogeneous microstructure.
drafts.intervention: Apply an optimized thermal aging treatment—at a temperature below the primary phase transformation (e.g., around 700–750°C) for a controlled duration in an inert atmosphere—to trigger the formation of coherent nano-scale gamma (Ti-Ni based) precipitates.
drafts.conditions: Testing and aging treatments are performed under conditions relevant to high-temperature applications (operating temperatures between 600°C and 900°C), with the aging conducted in an oxygen-free environment to avoid oxidation.
drafts.structural_mediator: Nano-scale precipitates that form along grain boundaries and within the matrix, thereby providing sites that pin dislocations and stabilize grain boundaries.
drafts.mechanism: The precipitates act as obstacles for dislocation movement and help reduce grain-boundary sliding at elevated temperatures, thereby enhancing yield strength and creep resistance via precipitation strengthening.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The thermally aged alloy is predicted to show a measurable improvement—such as an increase in yield strength (e.g., around 15% or more) and reduced creep rates—at high temperatures relative to the as-solution-annealed baseline.
drafts.baseline: The same titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy in the as-solution-annealed (non-aged) state.
drafts.boundary: The improvement is expected provided that: (1) all constituent elements remain within the high-entropy alloy composition limits (5–35 at%), (2) the aging temperature is sufficiently high to induce precipitate formation yet below any destabilizing phase transformation temperature, and (3) the alloy remains free of deleterious oxidation (i.e., treatment must be in an inert atmosphere).

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of specimens of the titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy that meets the high-entropy criteria. Subject one group to the thermal aging treatment (e.g., aging at 700–750°C for an optimized duration in an inert atmosphere) and leave the other group as the baseline (as-solution-annealed). Subsequently, conduct high-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., creep tests and yield strength measurements at around 800°C) on both groups.
measurements: Creep rate under a fixed load at high temperature
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to quantify precipitate density and distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis would be falsified if the aged specimens do not show a statistically significant (e.g., less than a 15% increase) improvement in yield strength and reduction in creep rate compared to the as-solution-annealed specimens, or if TEM reveals no increase in the formation of coherent nano-scale precipitates.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding small amounts (e.g., 3–5 at%) of a refractory element such as tungsten to a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy will form fine, coherent tungsten-rich precipitates that inhibit dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding at elevated temperatures, thereby improving its high-temperature mechanical strength and creep resistance compared to the alloy without tungsten.
drafts.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with titanium and nickel as primary constituents (with the other three or more elements each within 5–35 at%), without tungsten.
drafts.intervention: Introduce 3–5 at% tungsten into the alloy composition.
drafts.conditions: Elevated-temperature service conditions (e.g., testing temperatures ~800°C) and within the compositional boundaries typical for high-entropy alloys (individual element contents of 5–35 at%).
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of fine, coherent tungsten-rich precipitates distributed within the alloy matrix.
drafts.mechanism: The tungsten addition promotes the nucleation of fine precipitates that pin dislocations and restrict grain-boundary motion during high-temperature deformation, thus enhancing the alloy's elevated-temperature mechanical stability.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The tungsten-containing alloy is expected to exhibit increased yield strength and improved creep resistance at high temperatures relative to the baseline alloy without tungsten.
drafts.baseline: The titanium-nickel primary high-entropy alloy without tungsten addition.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable when the alloy is processed to maintain a uniform distribution of precipitates, and testing is conducted at temperatures around or above 800°C under stress levels typical of high-temperature applications.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys with identical base compositions, one set with 3–5 at% tungsten addition and the other without tungsten. Process both sets under identical conditions to achieve similar microstructures. Subject both alloy sets to high-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., creep tests or high-temperature compression tests) at around 800°C.
measurements: Yield strength or creep rupture strength at high temperatures
Creep strain rate under controlled stress
Microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM or SEM) to observe precipitate formation and distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-containing alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in high-temperature yield strength and/or creep resistance compared to the baseline alloy (or if detrimental phases form that adversely affect the properties), then the hypothesis is falsified.
